Before passing under [Tower Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_Bridge "Tower Bridge"), she lit the National Millennium Beacon in the [Pool of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pool_of_London "Pool of London") using a laser torch.[[174]](#cite_note-180) Shortly before midnight, she officially opened the Dome.[[175]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnappett201624-181) During the singing of *[Auld Lang Syne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auld_Lang_Syne "Auld Lang Syne")*, Elizabeth held hands with Philip and British prime minister [Tony Blair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Blair "Tony Blair").[[176]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShawcross2002224Bedell_Smith2017423-182) Following the [9/11 attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9/11_attacks "9/11 attacks") in the United States, Elizabeth, breaking with tradition, ordered the [American national anthem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_national_anthem "American national anthem") to be played during the [changing of the guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Changing_of_the_guard_(United_Kingdom) "Changing of the guard (United Kingdom)") at Buckingham Palace to express her solidarity with the country.[[177]](#cite_note-183)[[178]](#cite_note-184)

[![Six formally dressed guests, including Elizabeth II in a pale blue gown, pose in an ornate palace room.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Queen_Elizabeth_II_with_her_British_Prime_Ministers_during_her_Golden_Jubilee_in_2002.jpg/250px-Queen_Elizabeth_II_with_her_British_Prime_Ministers_during_her_Golden_Jubilee_in_2002.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Queen_Elizabeth_II_with_her_British_Prime_Ministers_during_her_Golden_Jubilee_in_2002.jpg)

With living British prime ministers during a [Golden Jubilee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Jubilee_of_Elizabeth_II "Golden Jubilee of Elizabeth II") dinner, 2002

In 2002, Elizabeth marked her [Golden Jubilee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Jubilee_of_Elizabeth_II "Golden Jubilee of Elizabeth II"), the 50th anniversary of her accession. Her sister died in February and [her mother in March](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_and_funeral_of_Queen_Elizabeth_the_Queen_Mother "Death and funeral of Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother"), and the media speculated on whether the Jubilee would be a success or a failure.[[179]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBond2006156Bradford2012248–249Marr2011349–350-185) Margaret's death shook Elizabeth; her funeral was one of the rare occasions where Elizabeth openly cried.[[180]](#cite_note-186) Elizabeth again undertook an extensive tour of her realms, beginning in Jamaica in February, where she called the farewell banquet "memorable" after a [power cut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_cut "Power cut") plunged [King's House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King's_House,_Jamaica "King's House, Jamaica"), the official residence of the [governor-general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor-General_of_Jamaica "Governor-General of Jamaica"), into darkness.[[181]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrandreth200431-187) As in 1977, there were street parties and commemorative events, and monuments were named to honour the occasion. One million people attended each day of the three-day main Jubilee celebration in London,[[182]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBond2006166–167-188) and the enthusiasm shown for Elizabeth by the public was greater than many journalists had anticipated.[[183]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBond2006157-189)

In 2003, Elizabeth sued the *[Daily Mirror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily_Mirror "Daily Mirror")* for [breach of confidence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breach_of_confidence_in_English_law "Breach of confidence in English law") and obtained an [injunction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Injunction "Injunction") which prevented the outlet from publishing information gathered by a reporter who posed as a [footman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footman "Footman") at Buckingham Palace.[[184]](#cite_note-190) The newspaper also paid £25,000 towards her legal costs.[[185]](#cite_note-191) Though generally healthy throughout her life, in 2003 she had [keyhole surgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keyhole_surgery "Keyhole surgery") on both knees. In October 2006, she missed the opening of the new [Emirates Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirates_Stadium "Emirates Stadium") because of a strained back muscle that had been troubling her since the summer.[[186]](#cite_note-192)

In May 2007, citing unnamed sources, *[The Daily Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Daily_Telegraph "The Daily Telegraph")* reported that Elizabeth was "exasperated and frustrated" by the policies of Tony Blair, that she was concerned the [British Armed Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Armed_Forces "British Armed Forces") were overstretched in Iraq and [Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_Republic_of_Afghanistan "Islamic Republic of Afghanistan"), and that she had raised concerns over rural and countryside issues with Blair.[[187]](#cite_note-193) She was, however, said to admire Blair's efforts to achieve [peace in Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_in_Northern_Ireland "Peace in Northern Ireland").[[188]](#cite_note-194) She became the first British monarch to celebrate a diamond wedding anniversary in November 2007.[[189]](#cite_note-195) On 20 March 2008, at the [Church of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Ireland "Church of Ireland") [St Patrick's Cathedral, Armagh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Patrick's_Cathedral,_Armagh_(Church_of_Ireland) "St Patrick's Cathedral, Armagh (Church of Ireland)"), Elizabeth attended the first [Maundy service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maundy_service "Maundy service") held outside England and Wales.[[190]](#cite_note-196)

[![Elizabeth II, carrying a handbag and umbrella, greets a man in a red jacket at an outdoor ceremony, surrounded by officials, with camera crews in the background.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/Presentation_of_Membertou_Portrait_to_Queen_Elizabeth_II.jpg/250px-Presentation_of_Membertou_Portrait_to_Queen_Elizabeth_II.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Presentation_of_Membertou_Portrait_to_Queen_Elizabeth_II.jpg)

Presentation of a [Henri Membertou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Membertou "Henri Membertou") portrait during her 2010 Canadian tour

Elizabeth addressed the UN General Assembly for a second time in 2010, again in her capacity as Queen of all Commonwealth realms and [Head of the Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_the_Commonwealth "Head of the Commonwealth").[[191]](#cite_note-UN-197) The [UN secretary-general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UN_secretary-general "UN secretary-general"), [Ban Ki-moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ban_Ki-moon "Ban Ki-moon"), introduced her as "an anchor for our age".[[192]](#cite_note-BBCUN-198) During her visit to New York, which followed a tour of Canada, she officially opened a memorial garden for British [victims of the 9/11 attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victims_of_the_9/11_attacks "Victims of the 9/11 attacks").[[192]](#cite_note-BBCUN-198) Elizabeth's 11-day visit to Australia in October 2011 was her 16th visit to the country since 1954.[[193]](#cite_note-199) By invitation of the [Irish president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_president "Irish president"), [Mary McAleese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_McAleese "Mary McAleese"), she made the first [state visit to the Republic of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_visit_by_Elizabeth_II_to_the_Republic_of_Ireland "State visit by Elizabeth II to the Republic of Ireland") by a British monarch in May 2011.[[194]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBradford2012253-200)

### Diamond Jubilee and milestones

[![Elizabeth II in a bright pink coat and matching hat greets a cheerful crowd waving Union Jack flags at a station, surrounded by officials and police.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Day_194_-_West_Midlands_Police_-_Royal_Diamond_Jubilee_Visit_%287555521830%29.jpg/250px-Day_194_-_West_Midlands_Police_-_Royal_Diamond_Jubilee_Visit_%287555521830%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Day_194_-_West_Midlands_Police_-_Royal_Diamond_Jubilee_Visit_(7555521830).jpg)

Visiting [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham "Birmingham") in July 2012 as part of the Diamond Jubilee tour

The [2012 Diamond Jubilee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Diamond_Jubilee "2012 Diamond Jubilee") marked 60 years since Elizabeth's accession, and celebrations were held throughout her realms, the wider Commonwealth, and beyond. She and Philip undertook an extensive tour of the United Kingdom, while their children and grandchildren embarked on royal tours of other Commonwealth states on her behalf.[[195]](#cite_note-201) On 4 June, Jubilee beacons were lit around the world.[[196]](#cite_note-202) On 18 December, Elizabeth became the first British [sovereign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign "Sovereign") to attend a peacetime [Cabinet meeting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_Kingdom "Cabinet of the United Kingdom") since [George III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_III "George III") in 1781.[[197]](#cite_note-203)

Elizabeth, who opened the [Montreal Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal_Summer_Olympics "Montreal Summer Olympics") in 1976, also opened the [2012 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Summer_Olympics "2012 Summer Olympics") and [Paralympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Summer_Paralympics "2012 Summer Paralympics") in London, making her the first [head of state to open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_people_who_have_opened_the_Olympic_Games "List of people who have opened the Olympic Games") two [Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") in two countries.[[198]](#cite_note-204) For the London Olympics, she portrayed herself in [a short film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy_&_Glorious "Happy & Glorious") as part of [the opening ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony "2012 Summer Olympics opening ceremony"), alongside [Daniel Craig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Craig "Daniel Craig") as [James Bond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Bond "James Bond").[[199]](#cite_note-205) On 4 April 2013, she received an honorary [BAFTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA "BAFTA") award for her [patronage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patronage "Patronage") of the film industry and was called "the most memorable [Bond girl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bond_girl "Bond girl") yet" at a special presentation at Windsor Castle.[[200]](#cite_note-206)

In March 2013, Elizabeth stayed overnight at [King Edward VII's Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Edward_VII's_Hospital "King Edward VII's Hospital") as a precaution after developing symptoms of [gastroenteritis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gastroenteritis "Gastroenteritis").[[201]](#cite_note-207) A week later, she signed the new [Charter of the Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charter_of_the_Commonwealth "Charter of the Commonwealth").[[202]](#cite_note-208) That year, because of her age and the need for her to limit travelling, she chose not to attend the biennial [Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Heads_of_Government_Meeting "Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting") for the first time in 40 years. She was represented at the [summit in Sri Lanka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Commonwealth_Heads_of_Government_Meeting "2013 Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting") by Charles.[[203]](#cite_note-209) On 20 April 2018, the Commonwealth heads of government announced that Charles would succeed her as Head of the Commonwealth, which the Queen stated as her "sincere wish".[[204]](#cite_note-210) She underwent [cataract surgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cataract_surgery "Cataract surgery") in May 2018.[[205]](#cite_note-211) In March 2019, she gave up driving on public roads, largely as a consequence of a car accident involving her husband two months earlier.[[206]](#cite_note-212)

[![Elizabeth II, in a bright blue coat and matching hat, speaks at an outdoor transparent lectern as blurred spectators frame the foreground.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Official_Opening_of_the_Borders_Rail_-_21086557488.jpg/250px-Official_Opening_of_the_Borders_Rail_-_21086557488.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Official_Opening_of_the_Borders_Rail_-_21086557488.jpg)

Opening the [Borders Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borders_Railway "Borders Railway") on the day she became the longest-reigning British monarch, 2015. In her speech, she said she had never aspired to achieve that milestone.[[207]](#cite_note-213)

On 21 December 2007, Elizabeth surpassed her great-great-grandmother, Queen Victoria, to become the longest-lived British monarch, and she became the [longest-reigning British monarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_monarchs_in_Britain_by_length_of_reign "List of monarchs in Britain by length of reign") and [longest-reigning queen regnant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_longest-reigning_monarchs "List of longest-reigning monarchs") and female head of state in the world on 9 September 2015.[[208]](#cite_note-214) She became the oldest living monarch after the death of [King Abdullah of Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdullah_of_Saudi_Arabia "King Abdullah of Saudi Arabia") on 23 January 2015.[[209]](#cite_note-215) She later became the longest-reigning current monarch and the [longest-serving current head of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_current_state_leaders_by_date_of_assumption_of_office "List of current state leaders by date of assumption of office") following the [death of King Bhumibol Adulyadej](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_of_King_Bhumibol_Adulyadej "Death of King Bhumibol Adulyadej") of Thailand on 13 October 2016,[[210]](#cite_note-216) and the [oldest current head of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_state_leaders_by_age "List of state leaders by age") on the [resignation of Robert Mugabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resignation_of_Robert_Mugabe "Resignation of Robert Mugabe") of Zimbabwe on 21 November 2017.[[211]](#cite_note-217) On 6 February 2017, she became the first British monarch to commemorate [a sapphire jubilee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapphire_Jubilee_of_Elizabeth_II "Sapphire Jubilee of Elizabeth II"),[[212]](#cite_note-218) and on 20 November that year, she was the first British monarch to celebrate a platinum wedding anniversary.[[213]](#cite_note-219) Philip had retired from his official duties as Elizabeth's consort in August 2017.[[214]](#cite_note-220)

### Pandemic and widowhood

[![A desktop monitor shows Elizabeth II on a video call from an ornate room, with a small participant window showing Cindy Kiro above the main video call window.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/A_private_audience_with_Her_Majesty_Queen_Elizabeth_II.jpg/250px-A_private_audience_with_Her_Majesty_Queen_Elizabeth_II.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:A_private_audience_with_Her_Majesty_Queen_Elizabeth_II.jpg)

[Virtual meeting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_meeting "Virtual meeting") with [Cindy Kiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cindy_Kiro "Cindy Kiro") during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), October 2021

On 19 March 2020, as the [COVID-19 pandemic hit the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_Kingdom "COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom"), Elizabeth moved to Windsor Castle and sequestered there as a precaution.[[215]](#cite_note-221) Public engagements were cancelled and Windsor Castle followed a strict sanitary protocol nicknamed "HMS Bubble".[[216]](#cite_note-222) On 5 April, in a televised broadcast watched by an estimated 24 million viewers in the United Kingdom,[[217]](#cite_note-223) Elizabeth asked people to "take comfort that while we may have more still to endure, better days will return: we will be with our friends again; we will be with our families again; we will meet again."[[218]](#cite_note-224) On 8 May, the 75th anniversary of [VE Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VE_Day "VE Day"), in a television broadcast at 9 pm—the exact time at which her father had broadcast to the nation on the same day in 1945—she asked people to "never give up, never despair".[[219]](#cite_note-225) In 2021, she received her first and second [COVID-19 vaccinations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_vaccinations "COVID-19 vaccinations") in January and April respectively.[[220]](#cite_note-226)

[Philip died](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_and_funeral_of_Prince_Philip,_Duke_of_Edinburgh "Death and funeral of Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh") on 9 April 2021, after 73 years of marriage, making Elizabeth the first British monarch to reign as a [widow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Widow "Widow") or widower since Queen Victoria.[[221]](#cite_note-227) She was reportedly at her husband's bedside when he died,[[222]](#cite_note-228) and remarked in private that his death had "left a huge void".[[223]](#cite_note-229) Due to the COVID-19 restrictions in place in England at the time, Elizabeth sat alone at Philip's funeral service, which evoked sympathy from people around the world.[[224]](#cite_note-230) It was later reported in the press that Elizabeth had rejected a government offer to relax the rules.[[225]](#cite_note-231) In her Christmas broadcast that year, which was ultimately her last, she paid a personal tribute to her "beloved Philip", saying, "That mischievous, inquiring twinkle was as bright at the end as when I first set eyes on him."[[226]](#cite_note-232)

[![Leaders and guests gather at a formal outdoor event on a blue carpet before white geodesic domes, with a G7 Cornwall 2021 sign in front.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Prime_Minister_Boris_Johnson_G7_Summit_Day_One_-_51242021245.jpg/250px-Prime_Minister_Boris_Johnson_G7_Summit_Day_One_-_51242021245.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prime_Minister_Boris_Johnson_G7_Summit_Day_One_-_51242021245.jpg)

With other [G7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G7 "G7") leaders during the [47th G7 summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/47th_G7_summit "47th G7 summit") in Cornwall, 2021

Despite the pandemic, Elizabeth attended the [2021 State Opening of Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_State_Opening_of_Parliament "2021 State Opening of Parliament") in May,[[227]](#cite_note-233) the [47th G7 summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/47th_G7_summit "47th G7 summit") in June,[[228]](#cite_note-234) and hosted US president [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") at Windsor Castle. Biden was the 14th US president that she had met.[[229]](#cite_note-235) In October 2021, Elizabeth cancelled a planned trip to Northern Ireland and stayed overnight at King Edward VII's Hospital for "preliminary investigations".[[230]](#cite_note-236) On Christmas Day 2021, while she was staying at Windsor Castle, 19-year-old Jaswant Singh Chail broke into the gardens using a rope ladder and carrying a [crossbow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossbow "Crossbow") with the aim of assassinating Elizabeth in revenge for the [Amritsar massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amritsar_massacre "Amritsar massacre"). Before he could enter any buildings, he was arrested and detained under the [Mental Health Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mental_Health_Act_2007 "Mental Health Act 2007"). In February 2023, Chail pleaded guilty to [attempting to injure or alarm the sovereign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treason_Act_1842#Section_2 "Treason Act 1842"),[[231]](#cite_note-237) and was sentenced in October to a nine-year custodial sentence plus an additional five years on extended licence. The sentencing judge also placed Chail under a hybrid order under section 45A of the [Mental Health Act 1983](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mental_Health_Act_1983 "Mental Health Act 1983"), ordering that he remain at [Broadmoor Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadmoor_Hospital "Broadmoor Hospital") to be transferred into custody only after receiving psychiatric treatment.[[232]](#cite_note-238)

### Platinum Jubilee and beyond

[Elizabeth's Platinum Jubilee celebrations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth's_Platinum_Jubilee_celebrations "Elizabeth's Platinum Jubilee celebrations") began on 6 February 2022, marking 70 years since her accession.[[233]](#cite_note-239) In her [accession day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accession_day "Accession day") message, she renewed her commitment to a lifetime of public service, which she had originally made in 1947.[[234]](#cite_note-240)

Later that month, Elizabeth fell ill with COVID-19 along with several family members, but she only exhibited "mild cold-like symptoms" and recovered by the end of the month.[[235]](#cite_note-241)[[236]](#cite_note-242) She was present at [the service of thanksgiving for her husband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Service_of_Thanksgiving_for_the_life_of_The_Duke_of_Edinburgh "A Service of Thanksgiving for the life of The Duke of Edinburgh") at Westminster Abbey on 29 March,[[237]](#cite_note-243) but was unable to attend both the annual [Commonwealth Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Day "Commonwealth Day") service that month[[238]](#cite_note-244) and the [Royal Maundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Maundy "Royal Maundy") service in April, because of "episodic mobility problems".[[239]](#cite_note-245) In May, she missed the [State Opening of Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Opening_of_Parliament "State Opening of Parliament") for the first time in 59 years. (She did not attend the state openings in 1959 and 1963 as she was pregnant with Andrew and Edward, respectively.)[[240]](#cite_note-246) Later that month she made a surprise visit to [Paddington Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paddington_Station "Paddington Station") and officially opened the [Elizabeth line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_line "Elizabeth line"), named in her honour.[[241]](#cite_note-247)

[![Elizabeth II in bright green stands with royal family members on a palace balcony, smiling in a formal, celebratory scene.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/Queen_Elizabeth_II_Platinum_Jubilee_2022_-_Platinum_Pageant_%2852124830349%29.jpg/250px-Queen_Elizabeth_II_Platinum_Jubilee_2022_-_Platinum_Pageant_%2852124830349%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Queen_Elizabeth_II_Platinum_Jubilee_2022_-_Platinum_Pageant_(52124830349).jpg)

With the royal family on the balcony of Buckingham Palace following the [Platinum Jubilee Pageant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platinum_Jubilee_Pageant "Platinum Jubilee Pageant"), June 2022

Elizabeth was largely confined to balcony appearances during the public jubilee celebrations, and she missed the [National Service of Thanksgiving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platinum_Jubilee_National_Service_of_Thanksgiving "Platinum Jubilee National Service of Thanksgiving") on 3 June.[[242]](#cite_note-248) On 13 June, she became the second-longest reigning monarch in history (among those whose exact dates of reign are known), with 70 years and 127 days on the throne – surpassing [King Bhumibol Adulyadej](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Bhumibol_Adulyadej "King Bhumibol Adulyadej") of Thailand.[[243]](#cite_note-249) On 6 September, she appointed her 15th British prime minister, [Liz Truss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Truss "Liz Truss"), at Balmoral Castle in Scotland. This was the only occasion on which Elizabeth received a new prime minister at a location other than Buckingham Palace.[[244]](#cite_note-250) No other British monarch appointed as many prime ministers.[[245]](#cite_note-251) Elizabeth's last public message was issued on 7 September, in which she expressed her sympathy for those affected by the [Saskatchewan stabbings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saskatchewan_stabbings "Saskatchewan stabbings").[[246]](#cite_note-252)

Elizabeth did not plan to [abdicate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdicate "Abdicate"),[[247]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrandreth2004370–371Marr2011395-253) though she took on fewer public engagements in her later years and Charles performed more of her duties.[[248]](#cite_note-254) She told Canadian governor-general [Adrienne Clarkson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Clarkson "Adrienne Clarkson") in a meeting in 2002 that she would never abdicate, saying, "It is not our tradition. Although, I suppose if I became completely gaga, one would have to do something."[[249]](#cite_note-255) In June 2022, Elizabeth met the Archbishop of Canterbury, [Justin Welby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justin_Welby "Justin Welby"), who "came away thinking there is someone who has no fear of death, has hope in the future, knows the rock on which she stands and that gives her strength."[[250]](#cite_note-256)

## Death

Main article: [Death and state funeral of Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_and_state_funeral_of_Elizabeth_II "Death and state funeral of Elizabeth II")

[![Pallbearers in tartan kilts carry a flower-topped, flag-draped coffin toward a black hearse.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/Queen%27s_Coffin_Loading_2022.jpg/250px-Queen%27s_Coffin_Loading_2022.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Queen's_Coffin_Loading_2022.jpg)

Elizabeth's coffin being loaded into a hearse outside the [Palace of Holyroodhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Holyroodhouse "Palace of Holyroodhouse"), 2022

On 8 September 2022, Buckingham Palace stated, "Following further evaluation this morning, the Queen's doctors are concerned for Her Majesty's health and have recommended she remain under medical supervision. The Queen remains comfortable and at Balmoral."[[251]](#cite_note-257)[[252]](#cite_note-258) Her [immediate family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immediate_family "Immediate family") rushed to Balmoral.[[253]](#cite_note-259)[[254]](#cite_note-260) Elizabeth died peacefully at 3:10 pm, aged 96.[[255]](#cite_note-261)[[256]](#cite_note-COD-262)[[257]](#cite_note-263) Her death was announced to the public at 6:30 pm,[[258]](#cite_note-264)[[259]](#cite_note-265) setting in motion [Operation London Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_London_Bridge "Operation London Bridge") and, because she died in Scotland, [Operation Unicorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_London_Bridge#Operation_Unicorn "Operation London Bridge").[[260]](#cite_note-266)[[261]](#cite_note-267) Elizabeth was the first monarch to die in Scotland since [James V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_V "James V") in 1542.[[262]](#cite_note-268) Her [death certificate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_certificate "Death certificate") recorded her cause of death as "[old age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_age "Old age")".[[256]](#cite_note-COD-262)[[263]](#cite_note-269) According to former prime minister [Boris Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Johnson "Boris Johnson")[[264]](#cite_note-270) and the biographer [Gyles Brandreth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyles_Brandreth "Gyles Brandreth"), she was suffering from a form of [bone marrow cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone_marrow_cancer "Bone marrow cancer"), which Brandreth wrote was [multiple myeloma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_myeloma "Multiple myeloma").[[265]](#cite_note-271)

On 12 September, Elizabeth's coffin was carried up the [Royal Mile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Mile "Royal Mile") in a procession to [St Giles' Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Giles'_Cathedral "St Giles' Cathedral"), where the [Crown of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_Scotland "Crown of Scotland") was placed on it.[[266]](#cite_note-272) Her coffin lay at rest at the cathedral for 24 hours, guarded by the [Royal Company of Archers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Company_of_Archers "Royal Company of Archers"), during which around 33,000 people filed past it.[[267]](#cite_note-273) On 13 September, the coffin was flown to [RAF Northolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Northolt "RAF Northolt") in west London, before continuing its journey by road to Buckingham Palace.[[268]](#cite_note-274) On 14 September, her coffin was taken in a military procession to [Westminster Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Hall "Westminster Hall"), where Elizabeth's body [lay in state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lay_in_state "Lay in state") for four days. The coffin was guarded by members of both the [Sovereign's Bodyguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign's_Bodyguard "Sovereign's Bodyguard") and the [Household Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Household_Division "Household Division"). An estimated 250,000 members of the public [filed past the coffin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queue_for_the_lying-in-state_of_Elizabeth_II "Queue for the lying-in-state of Elizabeth II"), as did politicians and other public figures.[[269]](#cite_note-275)[[270]](#cite_note-276) On 16 September, Elizabeth's children held [a vigil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vigil_of_the_Princes#Queen_Elizabeth_II "Vigil of the Princes") around her coffin, and the next day her eight grandchildren did the same.[[271]](#cite_note-secondvigil-277)[[272]](#cite_note-278)

[![Guards in red uniforms stand beside a coffin draped with the British royal standard on a red platform inside a grand church, as visitors watch and line up along the sides.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/Elizabeth_II_Lying-in-State_-_04.jpg/250px-Elizabeth_II_Lying-in-State_-_04.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Elizabeth_II_Lying-in-State_-_04.jpg)

Elizabeth lying in state at [Westminster Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Hall "Westminster Hall"), 2022

Elizabeth's [state funeral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_funerals_in_the_United_Kingdom "State funerals in the United Kingdom") was held at Westminster Abbey on 19 September, marking the first time a monarch's funeral service had been held there since that of [George II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_II_of_Great_Britain "George II of Great Britain") in 1760.[[273]](#cite_note-279) More than a million people lined the streets of [central London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_London "Central London"),[[274]](#cite_note-SkyN-Crowds-280) and the day was declared a holiday in several Commonwealth countries. In Windsor, a final procession involving 1,000 military personnel took place and was witnessed by 97,000 people.[[275]](#cite_note-BBC_News-2022-281)[[274]](#cite_note-SkyN-Crowds-280) Elizabeth's [fell pony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fell_pony "Fell pony") and two [royal corgis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_corgis "Royal corgis") stood at the side of the procession.[[276]](#cite_note-282) After a committal service at [St George's Chapel, Windsor Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_George's_Chapel,_Windsor_Castle "St George's Chapel, Windsor Castle"), Elizabeth's body was interred with her husband Philip's in the [King George VI Memorial Chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_George_VI_Memorial_Chapel "King George VI Memorial Chapel") later the same day, in a private ceremony attended by her closest family members.[[277]](#cite_note-283)[[275]](#cite_note-BBC_News-2022-281)[[278]](#cite_note-284)[[279]](#cite_note-285)

## Public image

Main article: [Personality and image of Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personality_and_image_of_Elizabeth_II "Personality and image of Elizabeth II")

### Beliefs, activities, and interests

[![Elizabeth II and a man in ceremonial robes stand outside a wooden building, with two men visible in the doorway behind them.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/Elizabeth_II_outside_Warburton_Presbyterian_Church%2C_1954.jpg/250px-Elizabeth_II_outside_Warburton_Presbyterian_Church%2C_1954.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Elizabeth_II_outside_Warburton_Presbyterian_Church,_1954.jpg)

With the moderator of the [Presbyterian Church of Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_of_Victoria "Presbyterian Church of Victoria") after service, 1954

Elizabeth had a deep sense of religious and [civic duty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civic_duty "Civic duty"), and took her [Coronation Oath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronation_Oath "Coronation Oath") seriously.[[280]](#cite_note-286) Aside from her [official religious role](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_the_United_Kingdom#Religious_role "Monarchy of the United Kingdom") as [supreme governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_governor "Supreme governor") of the [established](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_religion "State religion") Church of England, she worshipped with that church and with the national [Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland").[[281]](#cite_note-287) She demonstrated support for [inter-faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter-faith "Inter-faith") relations and met with leaders of other churches and religions, including five popes: [Pius XII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pius_XII "Pius XII"), [John XXIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_XXIII "John XXIII"), [John Paul II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Paul_II "John Paul II"), [Benedict XVI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benedict_XVI "Benedict XVI") and [Francis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Francis "Pope Francis").[[282]](#cite_note-288) A personal note about her faith often featured in her annual [Christmas Message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_Message "Christmas Message") broadcast to the Commonwealth. In 2000, she said:[[283]](#cite_note-289)

> To many of us, our beliefs are of fundamental importance. For me the teachings of Christ and my own personal accountability before God provide a framework in which I try to lead my life. I, like so many of you, have drawn great comfort in difficult times from Christ's words and example.

Elizabeth rarely gave interviews, and little was known of her political opinions, which she did not express explicitly in public. By convention, the monarch’s political views are neither asked about nor publicly disclosed. When *Times* journalist [Paul Routledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Routledge "Paul Routledge") asked her about the [miners' strike of 1984–85](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miners'_strike_of_1984–85 "Miners' strike of 1984–85") during a royal tour of the newspaper's offices, she replied that it was "all about one man" (a reference to [Arthur Scargill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Scargill "Arthur Scargill")),[[284]](#cite_note-BBCRoutledge1999-290) with which Routledge disagreed.[[285]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoutledge1994xiii-291) Routledge was widely criticised in the media for asking the question and claimed that he was unaware of the protocols.[[285]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoutledge1994xiii-291) After the [2014 Scottish independence referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Scottish_independence_referendum "2014 Scottish independence referendum"), Prime Minister [David Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Cameron "David Cameron") was overheard telling [Mayor of New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_New_York_City "Mayor of New York City") [Michael Bloomberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Bloomberg "Michael Bloomberg") that Elizabeth was pleased with the outcome, an incident for which Cameron later apologised.[[286]](#cite_note-292) She had arguably issued a public coded statement about the referendum by telling one woman outside Balmoral Kirk that she hoped people would think "very carefully" about the outcome. It emerged later that Cameron had specifically requested that she register her concern.[[287]](#cite_note-293)

[![Bronze statue of a Elizabeth II in regal attire with three corgi dogs at its base, standing on a stone pedestal in a park setting with trees in the background.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4b/Statue_with_Corgis_-_geograph.org.uk_-_8179761.jpg/250px-Statue_with_Corgis_-_geograph.org.uk_-_8179761.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Statue_with_Corgis_-_geograph.org.uk_-_8179761.jpg)

A [statue of Elizabeth in Oakham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statue_of_Elizabeth_II,_Oakham "Statue of Elizabeth II, Oakham"), erected in 2024 with three [royal corgis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_corgis "Royal corgis") her foot and base.

Elizabeth was [patron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patron "Patron") of more than 600 organisations and charities.[[288]](#cite_note-294) The [Charities Aid Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charities_Aid_Foundation "Charities Aid Foundation") estimated that Elizabeth helped raise over £1.4 billion for her patronages during her reign.[[289]](#cite_note-295) Her main leisure interests included [equestrianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horses_of_Elizabeth_II "Horses of Elizabeth II") and dogs, especially her [Pembroke Welsh Corgis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembroke_Welsh_Corgi "Pembroke Welsh Corgi").[[290]](#cite_note-296) Her lifelong love of corgis began in 1933 with [Dookie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dookie_(dog) "Dookie (dog)"), the first of many royal corgis.[[291]](#cite_note-297) Scenes of a relaxed, informal home life were occasionally witnessed; she and her family, from time to time, prepared a meal together and washed the dishes afterwards.[[292]](#cite_note-298)

### Media depiction and public opinion

In the 1950s, as a young woman at the start of her reign, Elizabeth was depicted as a glamorous "fairytale Queen".[[293]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBond200622-299) After the trauma of the Second World War, it was a time of hope, a period of progress and achievement heralding a "new [Elizabethan age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabethan_age "Elizabethan age")".[[294]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBond200635Pimlott2001180Roberts200082Shawcross200250-300) Lord Altrincham's accusation in 1957 that her speeches sounded like those of a "[priggish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prig "Prig") schoolgirl" was an extremely rare criticism.[[295]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBond200635Pimlott2001280Shawcross200276-301) In the late 1960s, attempts to portray a more modern image of the monarchy were made in the television documentary *[Royal Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Family_(film) "Royal Family (film)")* and by televising [Prince Charles's investiture as Prince of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Charles's_investiture_as_Prince_of_Wales "Prince Charles's investiture as Prince of Wales").[[296]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBond200666–67,_84,_87–89Bradford2012160–163Hardman201122,_210–213Lacey2002222–226Marr2011237Pimlott2001378–392Roberts200084–86-302) Elizabeth also instituted other new practices; her first royal walkabout, meeting ordinary members of the public, took place during a tour of Australia and New Zealand in 1970.[[297]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHardman2011213–214-303) Her wardrobe developed a recognisable, signature style driven more by function than fashion.[[298]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHardman201141-304) In public, she took to wearing mostly solid-colour [overcoats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overcoat "Overcoat") and decorative hats, allowing her to be seen easily in a crowd.[[299]](#cite_note-305) By the end of her reign, nearly one third of Britons had seen or met Elizabeth in person.[[300]](#cite_note-306)

[![Elizabeth II in a light blue overcoat greets spectators on a crowded city street with a celebratory crowd.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Walkabout_by_Her_Majesty_The_Queen%2C_Town_Hall_Square%2C_Grimsby_12th_July_1977_%28archive_ref_CCHU-4-1-9-2%29_%2826284940210%29.jpg/250px-Walkabout_by_Her_Majesty_The_Queen%2C_Town_Hall_Square%2C_Grimsby_12th_July_1977_%28archive_ref_CCHU-4-1-9-2%29_%2826284940210%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Walkabout_by_Her_Majesty_The_Queen,_Town_Hall_Square,_Grimsby_12th_July_1977_(archive_ref_CCHU-4-1-9-2)_(26284940210).jpg)

Performing a walkabout during an event to mark her Silver Jubilee, dressed in a solid-light blue overcoat and hat

At Elizabeth's Silver Jubilee in 1977, the crowds and celebrations were genuinely enthusiastic;[[301]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBond200697Bradford2012189Pimlott2001449–450Roberts200087Shawcross20021114–117-307) but, in the 1980s, public criticism of the royal family increased, as the personal and working lives of Elizabeth's children came under media scrutiny.[[302]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBond2006117Roberts200091-308) Her popularity sank to a low point in the 1990s. Under pressure from public opinion, she began to pay income tax for the first time, and Buckingham Palace was opened to the public.[[303]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBond2006134Pimlott2001556–561,_570-309) Although support for [republicanism in Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republicanism_in_Britain "Republicanism in Britain") seemed higher than at any time in living memory, republican ideology was still a minority viewpoint, and Elizabeth herself had high approval ratings.[[304]](#cite_note-310) Criticism was focused on the institution of the monarchy itself, and the conduct of Elizabeth's wider family, rather than her own behaviour and actions.[[305]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPimlott2001578-311) Discontent with the monarchy reached its peak on the death of Diana, Princess of Wales, although Elizabeth's personal popularity – as well as general support for the monarchy – rebounded after her live television broadcast to the world five days after Diana's death.[[306]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBond2006134Pimlott2001624–625-312)

In November 1999, [a referendum in Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Australian_republic_referendum "1999 Australian republic referendum") on the future of the [Australian monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_monarchy "Australian monarchy") favoured its retention in preference to an indirectly elected head of state.[[307]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHardman2011310Lacey2002387Roberts2000101Shawcross2002218-313) Many republicans credited Elizabeth's personal popularity with the survival of the monarchy in Australia. In 2010, Prime Minister [Julia Gillard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_Gillard "Julia Gillard") noted that there was a "deep affection" for Elizabeth in Australia and that another referendum on the monarchy should wait until after her reign.[[308]](#cite_note-314) Gillard's successor, [Malcolm Turnbull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_Turnbull "Malcolm Turnbull"), who led the republican campaign in 1999, similarly believed that Australians would not vote to become a republic in her lifetime.[[309]](#cite_note-315) "She's been an extraordinary head of state", Turnbull said in 2021, "and I think frankly, in Australia, there are more Elizabethans than there are monarchists."[[310]](#cite_note-316) Similarly, referendums in both [Tuvalu in 2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Tuvaluan_constitutional_referendum "2008 Tuvaluan constitutional referendum") and [Saint Vincent and the Grenadines in 2009](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Vincentian_constitutional_referendum "2009 Vincentian constitutional referendum") saw voters reject proposals to become republics.[[311]](#cite_note-317)

Polls in Britain in 2006 and 2007 revealed strong support for the monarchy,[[312]](#cite_note-318) and in 2012, Elizabeth's Diamond Jubilee year, her approval ratings hit 90 per cent.[[313]](#cite_note-319) Her family came under scrutiny again in the last few years of her life due to her son Andrew's association with convicted sex offenders [Jeffrey Epstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_Epstein "Jeffrey Epstein") and [Ghislaine Maxwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghislaine_Maxwell "Ghislaine Maxwell"), [his lawsuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuffre_v._Prince_Andrew "Giuffre v. Prince Andrew") with [Virginia Giuffre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Giuffre "Virginia Giuffre") amidst accusations of sexual impropriety, and her grandson Harry and his wife [Meghan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meghan,_Duchess_of_Sussex "Meghan, Duchess of Sussex")'s [exit from the working royal family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megxit "Megxit") and subsequent move to the United States.[[314]](#cite_note-320) Polling in Great Britain during the Platinum Jubilee, however, showed support for maintaining the monarchy[[315]](#cite_note-321) and Elizabeth's personal popularity remained strong.[[316]](#cite_note-322) As of 2021 she remained the third [most admired woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Most_admired_woman "Most admired woman") in the world according to the annual [Gallup poll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallup_poll "Gallup poll"), her 52 appearances on the list meaning she had been in the top ten more than any other woman in the poll's history.[[317]](#cite_note-323)

Elizabeth was portrayed in a variety of media by many notable artists, including painters [Pietro Annigoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pietro_Annigoni "Pietro Annigoni"), [Peter Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Blake_(artist) "Peter Blake (artist)"), [Chinwe Chukwuogo-Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinwe_Chukwuogo-Roy "Chinwe Chukwuogo-Roy"), [Terence Cuneo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terence_Cuneo "Terence Cuneo"), [Lucian Freud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucian_Freud "Lucian Freud"), [Rolf Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolf_Harris "Rolf Harris"), [Damien Hirst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damien_Hirst "Damien Hirst"), [Juliet Pannett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juliet_Pannett "Juliet Pannett") and [Tai-Shan Schierenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tai-Shan_Schierenberg "Tai-Shan Schierenberg").[[318]](#cite_note-324)[[319]](#cite_note-NPG1-325) Notable photographers of Elizabeth included [Cecil Beaton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Beaton "Cecil Beaton"), [Yousuf Karsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yousuf_Karsh "Yousuf Karsh"), [Anwar Hussein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anwar_Hussein_(photographer) "Anwar Hussein (photographer)"), [Annie Leibovitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annie_Leibovitz "Annie Leibovitz"), [Lord Lichfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Anson,_5th_Earl_of_Lichfield "Patrick Anson, 5th Earl of Lichfield"), [Terry O'Neill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_O'Neill_(photographer) "Terry O'Neill (photographer)"), [John Swannell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Swannell_(photographer) "John Swannell (photographer)") and [Dorothy Wilding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Wilding "Dorothy Wilding"). The first official [portrait photograph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrait_photograph "Portrait photograph") of Elizabeth was taken by [Marcus Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Adams_(photographer) "Marcus Adams (photographer)") in 1926.[[320]](#cite_note-NPG-326)

### Titles and styles

Elizabeth held many titles and honorary military positions throughout [the Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Commonwealth "The Commonwealth"), was sovereign of many orders in her own countries and received honours and awards from around the world. In each of her realms, she had a distinct title that follows a similar formula: *Queen of Saint Lucia and of Her other Realms and Territories* in [Saint Lucia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Saint_Lucia "Monarchy of Saint Lucia")[[321]](#cite_note-327), *Queen of Australia and Her other Realms and Territories* in Australia[[322]](#cite_note-328)[[323]](#cite_note-329)[[324]](#cite_note-330), etc. She was also styled *[Defender of the Faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defender_of_the_Faith "Defender of the Faith")*.

### Arms

See also: [Flags of Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flags_of_Elizabeth_II "Flags of Elizabeth II")

From 21 April 1944 until her accession, Elizabeth's arms consisted of a [lozenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lozenge_(heraldry) "Lozenge (heraldry)") bearing the [royal coat of arms of the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_coat_of_arms_of_the_United_Kingdom "Royal coat of arms of the United Kingdom") differenced with a [label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Label_(heraldry) "Label (heraldry)") of three points [argent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argent "Argent"), the centre point bearing a [Tudor rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tudor_rose "Tudor rose") and the first and third a [cross of Saint George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_of_Saint_George "Cross of Saint George").[[325]](#cite_note-331) Upon her accession, she inherited the various arms her father held as sovereign, with a subsequently modified representation of the crown. Elizabeth also possessed [royal standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heraldic_banner "Heraldic banner") and personal flags for use [in the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Standard_of_the_United_Kingdom "Royal Standard of the United Kingdom"), [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_standards_of_Canada "Royal standards of Canada"), [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_Personal_Australian_Flag "Queen's Personal Australian Flag"), [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_Personal_New_Zealand_Flag "Queen's Personal New Zealand Flag"), [Jamaica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_Personal_Jamaican_Flag "Queen's Personal Jamaican Flag"), and elsewhere.[[326]](#cite_note-332) Elizabeth approved her modified British arms on 26 May 1954.[[327]](#cite_note-333)
